content: Febrile seizures, which occur in children older than one month during episodes of fever, affect approximately 2-4% of children in Great Britain and the United States. About 30% of these children experience recurrent febrile seizures. To mitigate the adverse effects associated with continuous antiepileptic drug use, rapid-acting antiepileptics and antipyretics are often administered during subsequent fever episodes. This review evaluates the effectiveness and safety of prophylactic antiepileptic and antipyretic drugs, as well as other biologically plausible drug interventions, in preventing febrile seizures in children. For this updated review, databases such as the Cochrane Register of Studies (CRS Web), MEDLINE, and others were searched up to February 3, 2020. Randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials comparing antiepileptics, antipyretics, or other central nervous system-active agents with placebo, no treatment, or other interventions were included. Data were collected and analyzed independently by multiple reviewers, with seizure recurrence assessed at various time points (6, 12, 18, 24, 36, 48 months, and up to 5-6 years). Adverse effects and potential publication bias were also evaluated. The review included 42 articles describing 32 randomized trials, involving 4,431 participants. Fifteen interventions, including both continuous and intermittent prophylaxis, were analyzed. The methodological quality of most studies was moderate to poor. No significant benefit was observed for intermittent phenobarbital, phenytoin, valproate, pyridoxine, ibuprofen, or zinc sulfate compared to placebo or no treatment. Similarly, no significant benefit was found for diclofenac compared to placebo followed by ibuprofen, paracetamol, or placebo; continuous phenobarbital compared to diazepam; intermittent rectal diazepam compared to intermittent valproate; or oral diazepam compared to clobazam. Intermittent diazepam demonstrated a significant reduction in recurrent febrile seizures compared to placebo or no treatment at six months (risk ratio [RR] 0.64, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.48 to 0.85; moderate-certainty evidence), 12 months (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.84; moderate-certainty evidence), 18 months (RR 0.37, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.60; low-certainty evidence), 24 months (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.95; high-certainty evidence), 36 months (RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.85; low-certainty evidence), and 48 months (RR 0.36, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.89; moderate-certainty evidence). However, no benefit was observed at 60 to 72 months (RR 0.08, 95% CI 0.00 to 1.31; very low-certainty evidence). Continuous phenobarbital reduced seizure recurrence at six months (RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.83; moderate-certainty evidence), 12 months (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.70; low-certainty evidence), and 24 months (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.89; moderate-certainty evidence). However, no significant reduction was observed at 18 months (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.05) or at 60 to 72 months (RR 1.50, 95% CI 0.61 to 3.69; very low-certainty evidence). Intermittent clobazam, compared to placebo, showed a significant reduction in seizure recurrence at six months (RR 0.36, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.64; low-certainty evidence). However, this result was based on a single study with a high recurrence rate (83.3%) in the control group, and further replication is needed. Intermittent oral melatonin, when compared to intermittent diazepam, did not significantly reduce seizures at six months (RR 0.45, 95% CI 0.18 to 1.15; very low-certainty evidence). Intermittent oral levetiracetam, compared to placebo, significantly reduced recurrent seizures at 12 months (RR 0.27, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.52; very low-certainty evidence). Adverse effects were variably reported. Up to 30% of children treated with phenobarbital and 36% of those treated with benzodiazepines experienced adverse effects. Two studies reported lower comprehension scores in children treated with phenobarbital. Evidence of publication bias was identified in the meta-analyses of phenobarbital versus placebo at 12 months but not at six months, and for valproate versus placebo at 12 months. The methodological quality of most studies was low or very low, with inadequate randomization and allocation concealment, and a frequent comparison of treatment versus no treatment rather than treatment versus placebo, increasing the risk of bias. In conclusion, intermittent diazepam and continuous phenobarbital reduced recurrence rates of febrile seizures, but adverse effects were common, affecting up to 30% of children. The apparent benefit of clobazam in one trial requires replication. Levetiracetam showed promise with a favorable safety profile, but further research is needed. Given the generally benign nature of recurrent febrile seizures and the high prevalence of adverse effects associated with these drugs, families should be provided with adequate information about the benign nature of febrile seizures, first aid management, and access to medical services.
